newsitem.title: USA: Damage award against Cellpro is let stand.
newsitem.headline: Damage award against Cellpro is let stand.

text.p: A federal judge has denied a motion to set aside a $2.3 million jury award against CellPro Inc in a patent infringement lawsuit brought by Johns Hopkins University, Becton Dickinson and Co and Baxter International Inc.

Judge Roderick McKelvie of U.S. District Court in Delaware said CellPro had failed to prove its allegation that Johns Hopkins had unfairly obtained two patents for stem cell selection technology by misleading the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (PTO).

In a 14 page decision released to Reuters on Monday, McKelvie said, "To prove inequitable conduct, (it must be demonstrated)...that the patent holder submitted material false information to the PTO with the intent to deceive or mislead."

At issue is CellPro's bone marrow transplant system CEPRATE SC, which was approved for sale in the U.S. late last year by the Food and Drug Administration. CEPRATE is used to treat patients with breast cancer, multiple myeloma and lymphoma, and is also being tested as a possible treatment for viral diseases like AIDS, according to CellPro.
Johns Hopkins licensed its patents to Becton, which retained the diagnostic rights and sublicensed the treatment rights to Baxter.
On April 30, McKelvie is scheduled to hear plaintiffs' motions to triple the damages against CellPro for alleged willful infringement. The damages were awarded after a jury trial last month.
The plaintiffs also want an injuction that would block the sale of CEPRATE unless CellPro pays the plaintiffs $2,000 for each disposable unit sold.
CellPro spokeswoman Joann Reiter told Reuters that such a royalty "far exceeds our profit." CEPRATE sells for $4,300.
The plaintiffs are also seeking an injunction that would limit CellPro sales to customers obtained before March 12, the date damages were awarded.
Reiter said there would be an expedited appeal should an injunction be granted.
"CEPRATE is our flagship product. We are counting on this to lead to the development of future products," she said.
CellPro's stock was up 5/16 at 5-15/16 Monday afternoon, down from 12-1/4 a week before the trial of the patent suit began on March 4.
